sections.heading: Strings
sections.body:
Strings

Strings are used for storing text/characters.
For example, "Hello World" is a string of characters.
Unlike many other programming languages, C does not have a String type
to easily create string variables. Instead, you must use the char type and create
an array of characters to make a string in C:
Note that you have to use double quotes ("").
To output the string, you can use the printf() function together with the format specifier %s to tell C that we are now working with strings:

Example

Another Way Of Creating Strings

In the examples above, we used a "string literal" to create a string
variable. This is the easiest way to create a string in C.
You should also note that you can create a string with a set of characters. This example will
produce the same result as the example in the beginning of this page:

Example

Why do we include the \0 character at the end? This is
known as the "null terminating character", and must be included when creating
strings using this method. It tells C that this is the end of the string.

Differences

The difference between the two ways of creating strings, is that the first method is easier
to write, and you do not have to include the \0 character, as C will do it for
you.
You should
note that the size of both arrays is the same: They both have 13 characters
(space also counts as a character by the way), including the \0 character:

sections.body:
Strings - Special Characters

Because strings must be written within quotes, C will misunderstand this string,
and generate an error:
The solution to avoid this problem, is to use the backslash escape character.
The backslash (\) escape character turns special characters into string characters:
The sequence \" inserts a double quote in a string:

Example

The sequence \' inserts a single quote in a string:

Example

The sequence \\ inserts a single backslash in a string:

sections.heading: String Functions
sections.body:
String Functions

C also has many useful string functions, which can be used to perform
certain operations on strings.
To use them, you must include the <string.h> header file in your program:

String Length

For example, to get the length of a string, you can use the strlen() function:

Example

In the Strings chapter, we used sizeof to get the size of a string/array. Note that sizeof and strlen behaves differently, as sizeof also includes the \0 character
when counting:

Example

It is also important that you know that sizeof will always return the memory size (in bytes), and not the actual
string length:

Example

Concatenate Strings

To concatenate (combine) two strings, you can use the strcat() function:

Example

Note that the size of str1 should be large enough to store the result of the
two strings combined (20 in our example).
Note that the size of str1 should be large enough to store the result of the
two strings combined (20 in our example).

Copy Strings

To copy the value of one string to another, you can use the strcpy() function:

Example

Note that the size of str2 should be large
enough to store the copied string (20 in our example).
Note that the size of str2 should be large
enough to store the copied string (20 in our example).

Compare Strings

To compare two strings, you can use the strcmp()
function.
It returns 0 if the two strings are equal, otherwise a value that is not 0:

Example

Complete String Reference

For a complete reference of string functions, go to our C
<string.h> Library Reference.
sections.code:
#include <string.h>

char alphabet[] = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";printf("%zu",
 strlen(alphabet));

char alphabet[] = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";printf("%zu\n",
 strlen(alphabet)); // 26printf("%zu\n",
 sizeof(alphabet)); // 27

char alphabet[50] = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";printf("%zu\n",
 strlen(alphabet)); // 26printf("%zu\n", sizeof(alphabet)); //
 50

char str1[20] = "Hello ";char str2[] = "World!";//
 Concatenate
 str2 to str1 (result is stored in str1)strcat(str1, str2);//
 Print str1printf("%s", str1);

char str1[20] = "Hello World!";char str2[20];// Copy str1 to str2
 strcpy(str2, str1);// Print str2 printf("%s", str2);

char str1[] = "Hello";char str2[] = "Hello";char str3[] = "Hi";
 // Compare str1 and str2, and print the resultprintf("%d\n",
 strcmp(str1, str2)); // Returns 0 (the strings are equal)//
 Compare str1 and str3, and print the result
 printf("%d\n", strcmp(str1, str3)); // Returns -4 (the strings are not
 equal)
